entities.summary:
Saturnino Gatti (1463–1518) was an Italian painter and sculptor active in an early-Renaissance style.

Born in Florence, Italy, Gatti was trained by the renowned artist Domenico Ghirlandaio, who had worked for the Medici family, the dominant ruling dynasty in Florence at the time. Gatti's early work was heavily influenced by the classical style of ancient Greece and Rome, which was a hallmark of the early Renaissance.

During his career, Gatti collaborated with other prominent artists of the time, including Leonardo da Vinci, who is believed to have commissioned several works from the artist. Gatti's most famous work, a sculpture of a St. John the Baptist, is now housed in the Uffizi Gallery in Florence.

Gatti's artistic style was characterized by its use of classical motifs and its focus on the human form. His work was widely admired during his lifetime, and he was considered one of the leading artists of the early Renaissance.

Despite his significant contributions to the art world, Gatti's life was cut short when he died in 1518 at the age of 55. His legacy continued to be felt in the art world for centuries, however, and he remains one of the most important artists of the early Renaissance.

The most striking aspect of Gatti's life and work is the way in which his artistic style was shaped by the cultural and historical context in which he lived. His use of classical motifs and his focus on the human form reflect the dominant artistic trends of the time, while his collaborations with other prominent artists demonstrate his position at the forefront of the artistic movement.

In the end, Gatti's work serves as a testament to the enduring power of classical art and its ability to inspire and influence generations of artists to come.
